Methods applied The sampling for this study was made by collecting oriented hand samples at an average rate of five per outcrop, mainly from natural outcrops. From the 33 sampling localities which are listed with relevant data in Table 1 those numbered N1, N2,..., N24 with the exception of N5 and N16 represent Younger Granite occurrences. N5, N16 and N25-N31 are localities in the youngest volcanics, while N32 and N33 refer to two Cretaceous outcrops. Within each locality samples are numbered by additional numerals separated by a hyphen from the symbol of locality, e.g. N4-2 means the second sample of locality N4. A.C. demagnetization technique was applied and the measurements of magnetiza- tion were carried out with a high sensitivity JR-2 (Jelinek) spinner-, and a low sensi- tivity home-made astatic magnetometer, respectively. Data processing was made on a RAZDAN-3 computer. Both measurements and data processing were executed in Hungary using the instruments and facilities of the Department of Geophysics, E/StvSs University, Budapest. In a more refined interpretation of the magnetization the possibility of the presence of a stable low temperature CRM should also be considered. We believe that setting the value of ~95 relatively low for rejection is a safeguard that CRM affected localities are not used palaeomagnetically. According to MERRILL (1976) the only instant that the presence of a low tempera- ture chemical remanence can produce an erroneous magnetic direction is when it is formed predominantly during one magnetic field polarity. This case cannot be ex- cluded entirely but it is more likely for a secondary CRM to be acquired during the whole life of the rock thereby to compose of oppositely-directed magnetizations and eventually to have a very moderate effect on the total remanence (MERRILL, 1975). Twenty-nine normal and thirty-one reversed magnetizations were recorded. The site means in both groups exhibit a large dispersion. Fisher's precision measure (FISHER, 1953) is as low as k = 8,3 for the overall mean direction of RM. The samples were collected from andesites and dacites of lower Helvetian to upper Tortonian ages (PANT6 and MIK6, 1964). The distribution of the 87 localities sampled is shown on the map (Fig. 1). PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A STUDY OF THE PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE INTRODUCTION The Sudbury Irruptive has inspired a voluminous body of geological literature and yet its mode of orig in still remains enigmatic from many points of view. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. The rocks of both members are known to dip concordantly toward the centre of the structure and they are presently believed to be about 1700 m. y. old (Fairbairn et al., 1968). Previous studies on the paleomagnetism of the irruptive by Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963) pointed out that the mean directions of magnetiza­ tion in the south and north sections of the oval diverge appreciably from one another. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). A large proportion of th e paleomagnetic data previously reported by Sopher satisfy the norms imposed on the data reported in the present study and can legitimately be combined with them. None of the previous paleo­ magnetic interpretations can yet be disputed or corroborated in the light of the above analysis but their basis and the planning of future work to test them is undoubtedly established more firmly. When applied to the two samples representative of sector 3, the test suggests more strongly that the micro­ pegmatite and the norite are of the same paleomagnetic age . An explanation for the obvious divergence of the two means obtained for sector 6 was given earlier but an examination of Table 10 suggests another possibility. The micropegmatite means of sectors 3 an\i 6 have roughly the same declinations as their norite counterparts but tliey are appreciably steeper, similar to the other micropegmatite sector means rep­ resented by only one site mean. This suggests that a steeply dipping com­ ponent of chemical magnetization due to alteration may have been differen­ tially but systematically added to the primary thermoremanent component of magnetization in the micropegmatite. This hypothesis would be compatible with the generally greater magnetization inhomogeneity observed within indi­ vidual cores and sites of the micropegmatite. On the other hand, the hypoth­ esis is not incompatible with the suggestion made above that the norite has been disturbed prior to the formation of the micropegmatite because tectonic displacement and chemical alteration may both have contributed to the 30 degree divergence between the two means obtained for sector 6. In the laboratory several specimens were prepared from each sample for measurement under an astatic magnetometer with a maximum sensitivity of 9 x emu of moment per mm deflection. Trial specimens were subjected to the usual step-wise partial demagnetization procedure, and a best field selected for AF cleaning of the remaining specimens from each site. In general, soft secondary components were removed in peak fields of 100-200 Oe. The site mean directions after cleaning were calculated giving unit weight to samples. A number of sites were discarded because cleaning was ineffective judged by a random distribution of sample directions after cleaning. Others were discarded because they showed unusually large intensities due to suspected lightning strikes. The remaining cleaned mean site directions were classified into normal (N), reversed (R) and intermediate (I). Introduction The Late Cenozoic volcanics of Kenya and Tanzania form a vast alkali igneous province which extends northwards into Ethiopia and which spans a time from Miocene to Recent. This paper describes the results of a large scale reconnaissance survey of the volcanics involving 184 sites mainly south of the equator. Preliminary results from some of these sites were reported by Mussett, Reilly & Raja (1964), and a detailed account is given in an unpublished thesis by Reilly (1970). Introduction The Late Cenozoic volcanics of Kenya and Tanzania form a vast alkali igneous province which extends northwards into Ethiopia and which spans a time from Miocene to Recent. This paper describes the results of a large scale reconnaissance survey of the volcanics involving 184 sites mainly south of the equator. Preliminary results from some of these sites were reported by Mussett, Reilly & Raja (1964), and a detailed account is given in an unpublished thesis by Reilly (1970). A number of sites were discarded because cleaning was ineffective judged by a random distribution of sample directions after cleaning. Others were discarded because they showed unusually large intensities due to suspected lightning strikes. Easter Island is a small isolated outcrop of volcanic rock in the southeast Pacific (27.1øS, 109.2øW) located 1380 km west of Chile, the nearest continental land mass. The island rises from the Sala y Gomez ridge just east of the axis of the east Pacific rise. It is part of a chain of sea- mounts interpreted to be related to a 'hot spot' or 'mantle plume' generated during the last 10 m.y. within the Nazca lithospheric plate [Herron, 1972a]. Although well known as an archeological site, only cursory geological investigations have been made of the island [Chubb, 1933; Bandy, 1937; Baker, 1966]. All the studies recognized the existence of three distinct episodes of volcanism and named each for its major volcano: Poike, Rano Kau, and Terevaka. Baker [1966] determined the relative ages of events and classified Poike and Rano Kau as the older episodes with Terevaka, covering the major,part of the island, as the youngest event (Figure 1). An extensive number of once-active volcanic vents and pyroclastic centers, especially during the Terevaka episode, make it difficult to correlate itndividual flows across the island or to further delin- eate the volcanic stratigraphy. The lava flows are transitional between island tholeiites and alkali basalts with even the more basic rocks saturated in silica ( J. Clark, personal commu- nication, 1975). Easter Island is situated between marine mag- netic anomalies 2 and 3 [Herron, 1972b], and thus the sea floor in the vicinity of the island has a minimum age of 2 m.y. and a maximum age of 5 m.y. Sixty-five Terevaka episode lava flows were drilled along with four Poike episode flows. The usual sampling technique consisted of drill- ing four cores per flow and determining the geographic orienta- tion prior to breaking the sample free from the host rock. In five cases, only three usable samples were obtained. Each core was cut into two or more specimens. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of all the speci- mens was measured o a flux gate spinner magnetometer [Isaacson, 1974]. A four-axis tumbler with an alternating mag- netic field was used for demagnetization experiments [Doell and Cox, 1965a]. Two or more specimens from each flow were subjected to progressive step demagnetization at field levels of 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800 Oe. The optimum demagnetiza- tion level for each flow was that at which the test specimens were most closely clustered.

It consists of a variegated siltstone in the lower part and is highly calcareous in the upper part, where it ranges from silty limestone to large stromatolitic bioherms, which coalesce into biostromes in places. INTRODUCTION This paper describes paleomagnetic measurements and de- magnetization analyses of the Late Cambrian Point Peak Member of the Wilberns Formation of the Llano uplift area in Texas and compares the results with previous work. A survey of published early Paleozoic paleomagnetic pole positions for North America reveals their relative scarcity [McElhinny, 1973]. Thus a comparison between North American data and results from other continental blocks is hardly possible with- out new data, and theories for pre-Mesozoic relative drift between the major continents [Wilson, 1966; Dewey and Bird, 1970; McKerrow and Ziegler, 1972; and many others] lack adequate paleomagnetic evidence. DEMAGNETIZATION DATA In the paleomagnetic laboratory of the State University of Utrecht core specimens (2.2 cm height, 2.5 cm diameter) were drilled from the hand- samples. The measurements were carried out on the very sensitive Czech- oslovakian JR-3 spinner. The specimens were subjected to standard altemat- ing fields for separation of the various magnetization components. No ther- mal cleaning was applied since these standard AF demagnetizations turned out to be most useful and adequate. Pilot specimens (at least one of each site) were progressively demagnetized in lo-15 steps up to the maximum obtainable peak value of 3100 Oe. According to the experiences with these pilot demagnetizations all specimens were partially demagnetized in 8-10 steps in the appropriate AF range. The characteristic and secondary magne- tization components could be separated and their directions determined with the useful help of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967,1975) which show sequential changes of the magnetization vector upon demagneti- zation. New paleomagnetic data are presented from Tuscany and the Southern Alps (Italy). I = +43.3”, (ugs = 5.3’) and for Late Santonian to Early Campanian rocks (D = 342.7”, Z = +50.9”, a95 = 5.3”). Comparison of these new data with published data of Permian and younger age from the Southern Alps and from Umbria respectively, leads to conclusions about movements of crustal blocks North and South of the PO-basin. Further comparison of the data from the Northern Apennines with published Sardinian data seems to support that Sardinia belonged to the central Italian Peninsula until present times. It is argued that the Northern Apennines and the Vicentinian Alps belonged to the African plate and that their movements were defined by the opening history of the Atlantic. It was found, however, that during Late Cretaceous and again in Early Tertiary the two Italian crustal blocks must have been uncoupled to some degree. A paleomagnetic study of Triassic redbeds from fourteen sites within the Idaho- Wyoming overthrust belt and three sites from the adjacent stable foreland was undertaken in an attempt to decipher the origin of the arcuate shape of the thrust-fold belt in north- western Wyoming. This belt rises from beneath the Snake River lava plain in eastern Idaho and trends east-southeast into Wyoming. South of Jackson, Wyoming, the belt swings 45 to 70 degrees to trend almost due south into west-central Wyoming. The westernmost of these zones, called zone A (Lomond Zone) exhibits a Grenvillian continental basement unconformably overlain by a Lower Paleozoic autochthonous succession, which in turn is covered by a stack of transported slices of Lower Paleozoic sedimentary and ophiolitic sequences. Towards the top of the section black hematite-stained sandstones and thin hematite pebble conglomerate predominate. The total thickness of the Bradore strata ranges from 50 to 70 m; for example, at Otter Cove the type section consists of 48 m of medium-grained, purple cross-bedded sand- stones overlain by 15 m of black hematitic sandstones. In Canada Bay the Bradore Formation consists of a locally developed basal breccia, followed by white to grey, green and light purple arkoses and sandstones, with occasional pebble con- glomerate. Towards the top of the section black hematite-stained sandstones and thin hematite pebble conglomerate predominate. The total thickness of the Bradore strata ranges from 50 to 70 m; for example, at Otter Cove the type section consists of 48 m of medium-grained, purple cross-bedded sand- stones overlain by 15 m of black hematitic sandstones. The paleomagnetic interpretation will require a knowledge of the degree of severity and age of deformation of the Bradore sediments. lllthough much of zone A witnessed both subsidence and uplift during the deformations as- sociated with the Late Precambrian-Cambrian erogenic cycle and the more widespread Ordovician-Devonian cycle (Williams et al., 1974), the autoch- thonous Bradore unit remained stable until subsidence began with the Late Cambrian. Williams and Stevens (1974) have summarized the evidence con- firming that zone A belongs to the ancient continental margin of eastern North America. In this paper we present the results of a paleomagnetic in- vestigation of the Lower Cambrian Bradore sandstones in the Canada Bay area (Fig. l), which comprise one of the autochthonous units of zone A. The peridotite consists of harzburgite (80% olivine Fog,,, 18% orthopyroxene (enstatite), and l-2% chromiferous spine1 picotite) occasionally extensively serpentinized; some of the samples are composed of 50% or more of serpen- tine as in the case of the oriented sample 3-88-73, which is a serpentinite. The magnetite content increases with the amount of serpentinization. The dunite is composed of 8590% olivine FogO, some clinopyroxene (diopside), 2-5% chromite and less than 1% magnetite. In the dunite as well as in the peridotite, the magnetite content increases with serpentinization. The gabbros are layered and their average composition is 40-60% plagioclase (Ans5& and clino- pyroxenes (diopside and augite); these clinopyroxenes are commonly amphi- bolized (hornblende). Primary direc- tions of magnetisation show marked improvement in precision after correction for penecontemporaneous folding, and show a late Llandovery reversal in the sense R ~ N. The group mean directions of magnetisation is D = 243.5 ° , I = 47.5 ° (precision parameter k = 29). Petrographic examination confirms observations from magnetic properties that relict titanomagnetite (oxidation classes 3 to 5) is the remanence carrier in most samples. Hematite, probably mostly late magmatic in origin, is widely developed in all samples, but only the principal remanence carrier where it has thoroughly replaced the titanomagnetite. The mean virtual geomagnetic pole position is close to Upper Silurian/Lower Devonian pole positions from other parts of Britain and defines a minimum apparent polar shift of 60 ° between late Ordovician and Upper Llandovery times. Reference to absolute age dates suggests that this shift took place between ca. 447 and 434 m.y. followed by slight polar movement between ca. 434 and 394 m.y. 1. 7), Rose (1969), and Colemann-Saad (1969) described the geology of the area. Heyl and Ronan suggest that the Indian Head is a disconnected western edge of the Long Range massif. The complex is in the form of a broad dome with shallow dipping limbs, that plunge 15" to 30" NE. The dome structure is disrupted by a number of faults that strike north to northeast. Iron and titanium oxide deposits are associated with the anorthosite. A potassium-argon age determination is avail- able for a chlorite extract from the gabbroic anorthosite of the Steel Mountain complex (Leech et al. 1963), which gave an age of 451 f 35 m.y. Although Williams (1970) regarded the Steel Mountain complex as a Grenville inlier, he pointed out the obscurity of relationship of this anorthosite unit to the Paleozoic rocks. Recent geological work indicates an age of 1700 m.y., but this is not yet known with certainty. Results from 29 sampling sites stratigraphically covering the Tochatwi Formation are presented. Standard paleomagnetic techniques indicate that post- folding remagnetization is common, and this is confirmed by analysis of the magnetic vectors removed as partial thermal demagnetization proceeds. Two phases of remagnetization are recognized, one of which can be attributed to nearby Mackenzie-age intrusions. ihe other phase is equivalent to a remagnetization observed by other workers in Kahochella Group strata at localities70 km away. As yet, the source of this remagnetization event cannot be identified. Eight sampling sites have escaped total remagnetization and an earlier, pre-folding remanence has been isolated from these (D = 030, I = - 11, k = 14, a,, = 15"). One interesting point does emerge, however. Reference to figs. 2 and 8 in the companion paper (Binpham and Evans 1976) shows that the polarity of sites SEA and SEB, which occur at the very top of the Stark Formation, is normal (i.e. south- west and shallow). The same polarity is re- corded at sites FA and NA, which are separated laterally by some 14 km but which both lie in the bottom 20-40 m of the Tochatwi Formation. Between sites FA and FB, a reversal occurs indicating that the normal polarity magnetozone which starts near the top of the Stark Formation occupies a limited stratigraphic thickness and was therefore probably short-lived. The latter generally contain pyroxene, and plutons of pyroxene quartz-monzonite are particularly abundant within the anorthosite belt north of the Gren- ville Front. Secondary magnetizations could only be removed successfully through thermal demagnetization procedures and then only if the cleaning process was completed by 450°C. Heating in air caused extensive magnetochemical changes to occur above this temperature. Coercivity spectrum analysis and low-temperature characteristics of the heated and unheated green sediments indicate that considerable amounts of fine-grained single-domain magnetite are formed at 500°C or more from some non-magnetic mineral, probably the iron silicates. For this reason consistent palaeomagnetic data could only be obtained from about half the samples collected. Results from 4 sites (19 samples) of the Lower Sakamena Group give a palaeomagnetic pole at 64.9S, 1

compared with corresponding data from Africa these results confirm and strengthen our previous conclusions from the.Triassic-Jurassic Isalo Group regarding the palaeoposition of Madagascar. All three poles are only consistent with the Smith and HaUam reconstruction which places Madagascar off the eastern coast of Africa adjacent to Kenya and Tanzania. 1. Introduction and sampling In a previous paper [1] we presented some palaeo- magnetic results from the Triassic-Jurassic Isalo Group, the youngest group comprising the Malagasy Karroo Supergroup. In this paper we present results from the underlying Sakoa and Sakamena Groups; they reinforce our previous conclusions regarding the palaeoposition of Madagascar adjacent to Africa in the supercontinent of Gondwanaland. The geology of Madagascar has recently been re- viewed by Besairie [2] who has also provided a more detailed description of the sedimentary sequences of the island [3]. The Karroo Supergroup forms a con- tinuous north-south sedimentary belt on the western side, transgressively overlying the Precambrian crystal- line basement eastwards (see inset of Fig. 1). The basal Sakoa Group of Late Carboniferous to Early Permian 1 Now at: Division of Mineral Physics, C.S.I.R.O. Minerals Re- search Laboratories, P.O.

The Sakoa Group is overlain with an angular uncon- formity of about 10 ° by the Sakamena Group of Late Permian to Early Triassic age. The facies of the Sakoa and Sakamena Groups in the southwest are essentially continental, but contain important marine incursions. Introduction and sampling In a previous paper [1] we presented some palaeo- magnetic results from the Triassic-Jurassic Isalo Group, the youngest group comprising the Malagasy Karroo Supergroup. Introduction In the last few years, a series of palaeomagnetic data has been published which show an anticlockwise rotation of the Adriatic plate in the Tertiary. The data are based on measurements in several places throughout the Apennine peninsula and the Southern Alps and show rotation angles between 23° and 55° (Hargraves and Fischer, 1959; Van Hilten, 1960; Manzoni, 1970; Soffel, 1972; Zijderveld and Van der Yoo, 1973; Lowrie and Alvarez, 1974; Channell and Tarling, 1975; Channell and Horvath, 1976; Vandenberg and Wonders, 1976; Van der V oo and Zijderveld, 1969). The Austroalpine nappe system of the Eastern Alps is considered to have been part of the Adriatic plate which split off from the Eurasian continent due to the opening of the South Penninic ocean. Palaeomagnetism of the Svecofennian Loftahammar gabbro and some Jotnian dolerites in the Swedish part of the Baltic Shield. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 12: 51—64. The Svecofennian Loftahammar gabbro (Rb—Sr isochron age 1,694 - 106 year) and Jotnian dolerites (K—Ar iso- chron age 1,245 106 year) in Sweden were found to have palaeomagnetic pole positions in close agreement with poles from other Svecofennian rocks in Sweden and Jotnian dolerites in Finland, respectively. These results support Neuvonen’s apparent polar wandering path during the period from 1,900 lO~ to 1,300 106 year. A reconstruction of the position of the Baltic Shield during the (1,900—1,200) 106-year interval, based on avail- able pole positions, indicates that the Baltic shield was close to Greenland and the North American Shield and reveals a contiguity of North Atlantic geologic-geochronological zones until 1,200 106 year ago. 1. The Svecofennian Loftahammar gabbro (Rb—Sr isochron age 1,694 - 106 year) and Jotnian dolerites (K—Ar iso- chron age 1,245 106 year) in Sweden were found to have palaeomagnetic pole positions in close agreement with poles from other Svecofennian rocks in Sweden and Jotnian dolerites in Finland, respectively. These results support Neuvonen’s apparent polar wandering path during the period from 1,900 lO~ to 1,300 106 year. A reconstruction of the position of the Baltic Shield during the (1,900—1,200) 106-year interval, based on avail- able pole positions, indicates that the Baltic shield was close to Greenland and the North American Shield and reveals a contiguity of North Atlantic geologic-geochronological zones until 1,200 106 year ago. 1.
